---
title: "Accuracy of Polled Data in Predicting Presidential Results"
author:
  - "Patrick Brinkworth (a1966975)"
  - "Daniel O'Loughlin (a1968026)"
  - "Lachlan Ellis (a1971583)"
  - "Jasper Hill (a1973576)"
date: today
abstract: |
  Opinion polls are widely used to anticipate election results, but how reliable are they, and does the way a poll is run make a difference? We studied 2,424 state-level presidential polls from the 2012 and 2016 US elections, comparing each poll's predicted lead with the actual result in that state. Using regression models, we examined whether polling mode, the population sampled, who ran the poll, sample size and how close to election day the poll was taken could explain accuracy, and tested how well these models could predict the accuracy of polls they had not seen. Polling accuracy was associated with how close to election day a poll was conducted and its mode, while sample size and partisanship were also associated with accuracy in 2016, but all of these factors together explained only about 6% of the variation in polling error. The models predicted the accuracy of new polls little better than a simple average, suggesting that most polling error is random or caused by factors not captured in our data, so a poll's method alone is a poor guide to how far it can be trusted.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(tidyverse) # General functions
library(car) # Has capital A Anova
library(rsample) # Allows us to do train test split
library(knitr)
library(modelsummary)
set.seed(67) # Set the seed 
```

```{r}
#| label: data-prep
#| include: false
polls <- read.csv("Data/Clean/combined_data.csv") %>% 
  filter(sample_size > 0, sample_subpopulation != "Adults") %>% # drops the polls whose invalid sample_size (-1) was set to NA, and the very few Adult observations
  mutate(abs_err = abs((dem - rep) - act_margin), # how far off the poll was
         correct = if_else(dem == rep, NA_integer_, # did the poll pick the right winner?
                           as.integer(sign(dem - rep) == sign(act_margin))),
         n1000   = sample_size / 1000, # Sample size in thousands (easier to interpret coefficients)
         partisanship = factor(partisanship))
# Number of polls, quoted in the text
n_polls <- nrow(polls)
n_all12 <- sum(polls$year == 2012)
n_all16 <- sum(polls$year == 2016)
```

```{r}
#| label: prep-split
#| include: false
# Separate the elections; modes with fewer than 30 polls in a year are grouped as "Other"
# and Live Phone is the reference level
prep <- function(yr) { 
  polls %>% filter(year == yr) %>% # Datasets are joined, separate by year
    mutate(mode3 = fct_lump_min(factor(mode), min = 30, other_level = "Other"), # All modes with less than 30 polls put in other
           mode3 = relevel(mode3, ref = "Live Phone")) %>% #Reorder mode 
    droplevels()
}
all12 <- prep(2012)
all16 <- prep(2016)
```

```{r}
#| label: tt16
#| include: false

set.seed(67)

# 75/25 train test split
split12 <- initial_split(all12, prop = 0.75)
split16 <- initial_split(all16, prop = 0.75)

# Extract training and testing datasets
d12 <- training(split12)
test12  <- testing(split12)

d16 <- training(split16)
test16  <- testing(split16)

# Signed error for data correcting 
d12s <- d12 %>% 
  mutate(
  signed_err = ((dem-rep) - act_margin)
)

d16s <- d16 %>% 
  mutate(
  signed_err = ((dem-rep) - act_margin)
)

```


# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Our goal is to understand the accuracy of polls in political situations. More explicitly, we ask: how well can the accuracy of a poll be predicted based on the sampled population? We consider accuracy in two ways, the size of the error in a poll's predicted margin, and whether the poll correctly identifies the winning candidate. Biases in polls can lead to inaccurate reporting leading up to elections, and could influence the voting habits of prospective voters. Treating polls as objectively correct can lead to reduced trust in polls and incorrect results in significant elections can shake public confidence in polls [@pew2018]. For example, in 2016 state polls underestimated support for Donald Trump in several pivotal states [@kennedy2018], partially due to the biases of the sampled subpopulations. We begin to answer this question  by asking how different methods and factors in a polled population affect the accuracy of polls. Finally, once we've found out the accuracy of our polls, we consider the impact of unexpected results on the accuracy of prediction. Research has found that error can depend on who is sampled and how, as well as how undecided voters are treated [@bon2019]. Understanding which characteristics are associated with polling errors may help identify limitations in current polling methods and inform future analyses.



# Methods {#sec-method}



## Data

Our data consists of three datasets, polling information from 2012 and 2016, as well as presidential election results from 1976-2024. The 2012 and 2016 datasets contain state-level polling information collected by HuffPost Pollster from a range of polling organisations prior to each election, and the 1976–2024 dataset contains certified presidential election results sourced from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab. Further details about cleaning choices and their limitations can be found in the EDA report.

After removing two polls with an invalid sample size and 12 polls of adults, each of the `r n_polls` polls (`r n_all12` in 2012 and `r n_all16` in 2016) is compared with the actual result for its state. We measure accuracy in two ways. The *absolute margin error* is the number of percentage points by which a poll's Democrat-minus-Republican lead differed from the actual margin. We use the margin rather than each candidate's share because undecided respondents mean a candidate's poll percentage sits below their vote share even for a perfect poll, which the margin cancels out. The binary outcome *correct* records whether the poll's leader won the state (exact ties are excluded because they predict no winner).

The predictors are polling mode, sampled population, partisanship, sample size (per 1000 respondents) and days to election. Modes with fewer than 30 polls in a year are grouped as "Other" (@tbl-modes), and Live Phone is the reference level, so each mode coefficient is a difference from a live-phone poll.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-modes
#| tbl-cap: "Number of polls by polling mode in each election. Modes with fewer than 30 polls in a year are grouped as Other."
bind_rows(all12, all16) %>%
  count(year, mode3) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Mode", "2012", "2016"))
```


## Statistical methods

The 2012 and 2016 elections are analysed separately due to differences in their modes and voting trends. In each year, 25% of polls were held out as a test set (seed 67) and all models are fitted to the remaining 75%. The testing polls assess predictive performance.

We use linear regression to investigate how the selected characteristics relate to the magnitude of polling error. Logistic regression is used separately to investigate whether these characteristics can predict if a poll identifies the correct winner.

We fit a multiple linear regression of absolute margin error on all five predictors. Each predictor is tested with a Type II F-test (done through ANOVA) and multicollinearity is checked with generalised variance inflation factors (GVIFs). Stepwise selection by AIC identifies simpler models. We check the assumptions of linearity, constant variance and normal residuals with residual and Q-Q plots, and look for influential polls using Cook's distance and studentised residuals above 3. We also conduct a sensitivity analysis by refitting the linear models after excluding influential training polls identified by these diagnostic measures, and unexpected polls (greater than three residual standard errors from the model's prediction) from the testing polls. Because absolute errors are right-skewed, a Box-Cox analysis chooses a power transformation of the response.

We model `correct` with logistic regression on the same predictors. The "Other" mode is excluded because all of its 2012 polls were correct, which causes complete separation (its odds ratio cannot be estimated); we also exclude it in 2016 for comparability.

We also fit linear models of signed error (poll margin minus actual margin) to test whether polls could be adjusted for bias, comparing them with subtracting the training mean error, using a paired t-test on absolute errors. Linear predictive performance is summarised by mean absolute error (MAE) and out-of-sample R² (relative to predicting the training mean), and logistic performance by accuracy, majority-class accuracy and AUC. Partisanship records whether a poll was Non-partisan or run by a partisan Pollster or Sponsor.

Data preparation code is in @sec-app-data and the software environment can be found in @sec-app-env.

# Results {#sec-results}


```{r}
#| label: lmfit
#| include: false
# Full, intercept-only and all two way interaction models for each election
full12 <- lm(abs_err ~ mode3 + sample_subpopulation + partisanship + n1000 + days_to_election, data = d12)
null12 <- lm(abs_err ~ 1, data = d12)
full12_int <- lm(abs_err ~ (mode3 + sample_subpopulation + partisanship + n1000 + days_to_election)^2, data = d12)

full16 <- lm(abs_err ~ mode3 + sample_subpopulation + partisanship + n1000 + days_to_election, data = d16)
null16 <- lm(abs_err ~ 1, data = d16)
full16_int <- lm(abs_err ~ (mode3 + sample_subpopulation + partisanship + n1000 + days_to_election)^2, data = d16)
```

```{r}
#| label: lmtests
#| include: false
# Type II tests, multicollinearity (GVIF) and the anova against the null model
a12 <- Anova(full12, type = 2)
a16 <- Anova(full16, type = 2)
v12 <- vif(full12)
v16 <- vif(full16)
nested12 <- anova(null12, full12)
nested16 <- anova(null16, full16)
```

```{r}
#| label: lmselect
#| include: false
# Stepwise selection by AIC, over main effects and over all two way interactions
step12 <- step(null12, scope = list(lower = ~ 1, upper = formula(full12)), direction = "both", trace = 0)
step12_int <- step(null12, scope = list(lower = ~ 1, upper = formula(full12_int)), direction = "both", trace = 0)
step16 <- step(null16, scope = list(lower = ~ 1, upper = formula(full16)), direction = "both", trace = 0)
step16_int <- step(null16, scope = list(lower = ~ 1, upper = formula(full16_int)), direction = "both", trace = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: lminfluence
#| include: false
# Influence checks. studentised residual > 3, Cook's distance above 4/n, and the largest Cook's distance
diag_stats <- function(m) {
  list(n_rstud  = sum(abs(rstudent(m)) > 3),
       n_cook   = sum(cooks.distance(m) > 4 / nobs(m)),
       max_cook = max(cooks.distance(m)))   # worry if > 0.5 or 1
}
ds12 <- diag_stats(full12)
ds16 <- diag_stats(full16)
```

```{r}
#| label: sq2-influence
#| include: false
#Calculate influence measures for each training poll
influence_df <- function(model, data) {
data %>%
mutate(
fitted = fitted(model),
stud = rstudent(model),
cooks = cooks.distance(model),
outlier = abs(stud) > 3,
influential = cooks > 4 / nrow(data)
)
}
#Calculate for each election
inf12 <- influence_df(full12, d12)
inf16 <- influence_df(full16, d16)
```

```{r}
#| label: sq2-sensitivity
#| include: false

# MAE, RMSE and R² measured against a baseline prediction `base`.
# With base = the training mean this is the out-of-sample R² (negative = worse than the mean).
score <- function(y, pred, base) {
  ok <- !is.na(y) & !is.na(pred)
  y <- y[ok]
  pred <- pred[ok]
  c(MAE  = mean(abs(y - pred)),
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((y - pred)^2)),
    R2   = 1 - sum((y - pred)^2) / sum((y - base)^2))
}

sensitivity <- function(model, train, test, inf, year) {
# Refit without potentially influential training polls
trimmed <- lm(
formula(model),
data = train[!inf$influential, ]
)
# Identify unexpected test observations
unexpected <- abs(
test$abs_err - predict(model, test)
) > 3 * sigma(model)
# Training mean used as the R-squared baseline
base <- mean(train$abs_err)
# Function to evaluate predictive performance
evaluate <- function(m, training, keep) {
predictions <- predict(m, test[keep, ])
actual <- test$abs_err[keep]
bind_cols(
tibble(
Year = year,
`Training data` = training,
`Test data` = if (all(keep)) "All polls"
else "Without outliers",
Polls = length(actual)
),
as_tibble_row(
score(actual, predictions, base)
)
)
}
# Compare original and refitted models
bind_rows(
evaluate(
model, "All polls",
rep(TRUE, nrow(test))
),
evaluate(
model, "All polls",
!unexpected
),
evaluate(
trimmed, "Without influential",
rep(TRUE, nrow(test))
),
evaluate(
trimmed, "Without influential",
!unexpected
)
)
}
#Perform sensitivity analysis for both elections
s12 <- sensitivity(full12, d12, test12, inf12, "2012")
s16 <- sensitivity(full16, d16, test16, inf16, "2016")
```


```{r}
#| label: boxcox
#| include: false
# Box-Cox: estimated power with Wald confidence interval for each election
pt12 <- powerTransform(full12)
pt16 <- powerTransform(full16)
bc12 <- summary(pt12)$result   # columns: estimate, rounded power, lower and upper bound
bc16 <- summary(pt16)$result

# Estimates are close to 0.5, so refit with the square root for easier interpretation
full12_t <- update(full12, sqrt(abs_err) ~ .)
full16_t <- update(full16, sqrt(abs_err) ~ .)
```

```{r}
#| label: logitfit
#| include: false
# Logistic models for picking the right winner ("Other" mode excluded)
l12 <- d12 %>% filter(!is.na(correct), mode3 != "Other") %>% droplevels()
l16 <- d16 %>% filter(!is.na(correct), mode3 != "Other") %>% droplevels()

g12 <- glm(correct ~ mode3 + sample_subpopulation + partisanship + n1000 + days_to_election, family = binomial, data = l12)
g16 <- glm(correct ~ mode3 + sample_subpopulation + partisanship + n1000 + days_to_election, family = binomial, data = l16)

glm_a12 <- Anova(g12, type = 2)   # likelihood-ratio test for each predictor
glm_a16 <- Anova(g16, type = 2)
glm_null12 <- anova(glm(correct ~ 1, family = binomial, data = l12), g12, test = "Chisq")   # overall test
glm_null16 <- anova(glm(correct ~ 1, family = binomial, data = l16), g16, test = "Chisq")

# Proportion of polls that picked the right winner (%)
pct12 <- round(100 * mean(l12$correct), 2)
pct16 <- round(100 * mean(l16$correct), 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: functions
#| include: false
# Area under the ROC curve: the chance a random right-winner poll gets a higher predicted
# probability than a random wrong-winner poll (0.5 = no better than guessing)
auc <- function(y, p) {
  r <- rank(p)
  n1 <- sum(y == 1)
  n0 <- sum(y == 0)
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

# Predictions on the original (percentage point) scale. For a square-root model, E[Z^2] = mu^2 + sigma^2,
# so the residual variance is added back to avoid under predicting after back transforming.
pred_abs <- function(m, newdata, sqrt_scale = FALSE) {
  p <- predict(m, newdata = newdata)
  if (sqrt_scale) p^2 + sigma(m)^2 else p
}
```

```{r}
#| label: testeval
#| include: false
# Linear --- training vs test performance
eval_abs <- function(train, test, mods, yr) {
  base <- mean(train$abs_err)            # "predict the training mean" baseline
  one <- function(label, set, data, pred) {
    bind_cols(tibble(Year = yr, Model = label, Set = set),
              as_tibble_row(score(data$abs_err, pred, base)))
  }
  bind_rows(
    one("Training mean", "Train", train, rep(base, nrow(train))),
    one("Training mean", "Test",  test,  rep(base, nrow(test))),
    bind_rows(lapply(names(mods), function(nm) {
      sq <- nm == "Full (square root)"
      bind_rows(one(nm, "Train", train, pred_abs(mods[[nm]], train, sq)),
                one(nm, "Test",  test,  pred_abs(mods[[nm]], test,  sq)))
    }))
  )
}

lm_eval <- bind_rows(
  eval_abs(d12, test12, list(Full = full12, Stepwise = step12, "Full (square root)" = full12_t), "2012"),
  eval_abs(d16, test16, list(Full = full16, Stepwise = step16, "Full (square root)" = full16_t), "2016")
)

# Logistic --- performance on the test polls
# "Other" mode polls are dropped because the logistic models were fitted without them
prep_logit_test <- function(model, test) {
  test <- test %>% filter(!is.na(correct), mode3 != "Other")
  test$p <- predict(model, newdata = test, type = "response")   # predicted P(poll picks the right winner)
  test
}

logit_scores <- function(model, lt, yr) {
  major <- as.integer(mean(model$y) >= 0.5)   # majority class in the training data
  tibble(Year = yr,
         Polls = nrow(lt),
         Accuracy = mean((lt$p > 0.5) == lt$correct),
         `Majority-class accuracy` = mean(major == lt$correct),   # always predict the majority class
         AUC = auc(lt$correct, lt$p))
}

conf_df <- function(lt, yr) {
  lv <- c("Wrong winner", "Right winner")
  tibble(Predicted = factor(if_else(lt$p > 0.5, lv[2], lv[1]), levels = lv),
         Actual    = factor(if_else(lt$correct == 1, lv[2], lv[1]), levels = lv)) %>%
    count(Predicted, Actual, .drop = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(Year = yr)
}

lt12 <- prep_logit_test(g12, test12)
lt16 <- prep_logit_test(g16, test16)
logit_eval <- bind_rows(logit_scores(g12, lt12, "2012"), logit_scores(g16, lt16, "2016"))
conf_tab   <- bind_rows(conf_df(lt12, "2012"), conf_df(lt16, "2016"))

null_g12 <- glm(correct ~ 1, family = binomial, data = l12)
null_g16 <- glm(correct ~ 1, family = binomial, data = l16)

sg12 <- step(glm(correct ~ 1, family = binomial, data = l12),
             scope = list(lower = ~ 1, upper = formula(g12)), direction = "both", trace = 0)
sg16 <- step(glm(correct ~ 1, family = binomial, data = l16),
             scope = list(lower = ~ 1, upper = formula(g16)), direction = "both", trace = 0)

# All two-way interactions, then stepwise over them
g12_int <- glm(correct ~ (mode3 + sample_subpopulation + partisanship + n1000 + days_to_election)^2, family = binomial, data = l12)

g16_int <- glm(correct ~ (mode3 + sample_subpopulation + partisanship + n1000 + days_to_election)^2, family = binomial, data = l16)

sg12_int <- step(glm(correct ~ 1, family = binomial, data = l12),
             scope = list(lower = ~ 1, upper = formula(g12_int)), direction = "both", trace = 0)
sg16_int <- step(glm(correct ~ 1, family = binomial, data = l16),
             scope = list(lower = ~ 1, upper = formula(g16_int)), direction = "both", trace = 0)

logit_eval <- bind_rows(
  logit_scores(g12,  lt12, "2012") %>% mutate(Model = "Full"),
  logit_scores(sg12, prep_logit_test(sg12, test12), "2012") %>% mutate(Model = "Stepwise"),
  logit_scores(sg12_int, prep_logit_test(sg12_int, test12), "2012") %>% mutate(Model = "Interaction + Stepwise"),
  logit_scores(g16,  lt16, "2016") %>% mutate(Model = "Full"),
  logit_scores(sg16, prep_logit_test(sg16, test16), "2016") %>% mutate(Model = "Stepwise"),
  logit_scores(sg16_int, prep_logit_test(sg16_int, test16), "2016") %>% mutate(Model = "Interaction + Stepwise")
) %>% relocate(Model, .after = Year)

```

## Size of the polling error

```{r}
#| label: fig-days
#| fig-cap: "Absolute margin error against days to election in each election, by election. Each point is one poll; lines show fitted linear trends with 95% confidence interval."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
bind_rows(d12, d16) %>%
  ggplot(aes(days_to_election, abs_err)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(x = "Days to election", y = "Absolute margin error (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

@fig-days shows each poll's error against how many days before the election it ended. Most polls missed the margin by less than 10 points, but errors reached more than 30 points, and they were visibly more spread out in 2016 than in 2012. Errors tended to be larger for polls that ended earlier, as the fitted lines slope upwards in both elections. The wide scatter however, suggests that timing alone leaves most of the variation unexplained.

@tbl-anova gives the Type II F-test for each predictor and @tbl-lm the coefficients.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-anova
#| tbl-cap: "Type II ANOVA of absolute margin error on poll characteristics (training polls). Each F-test is adjusted for all other predictors."
# Descriptive predictor names
pred_lab <- c(
  mode3 = "Polling Mode",
  sample_subpopulation = "Voter Subpopulation",
  partisanship = "Partisanship",
  n1000 = "Sample Size (per 1,000)",
  days_to_election = "Days to Election"
)

# One row per predictor and election
anova_df <- function(a, yr) {
  a <- a[rownames(a) != "Residuals", ]

  tibble(
    Year = yr,
    Predictor = unname(pred_lab[rownames(a)]),
    Fstat = a[["F value"]],
    p = format.pval(a[["Pr(>F)"]], digits = 2, eps = 0.001)
  )
}

bind_rows(
  anova_df(a12, "2012"),
  anova_df(a16, "2016")
) %>%
  kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Year", "Predictor", "F", "p-value")
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lm
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of absolute margin error (percentage points) on poll characteristics (training polls). Standard errors in parentheses; reference levels are Live Phone, Likely Voters and Non-partisan."
coef_map <- c(
  "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
  "mode3Automated Phone" = "Automated Phone",
  "mode3Internet" = "Internet",
  "mode3IVR/Online" = "IVR/Online",
  "mode3IVR/Live Phone" = "IVR/Live Phone",
  "mode3Other" = "Other",
  "sample_subpopulationRegistered Voters" = "Registered Voters",
  "partisanshipPollster" = "Pollster",
  "partisanshipSponsor" = "Sponsor",
  "n1000" = "Sample Size (per 1,000)",
  "days_to_election" = "Days to Election"
)

modelsummary(
  list("2012" = full12, "2016" = full16),
  coef_map = coef_map,
  stars = TRUE,
  gof_map = tribble(
    ~raw, ~clean, ~fmt,
    "nobs", "Observations", 0,
    "r.squared", "R²", 3,
    "adj.r.squared", "Adjusted R²", 3
  )
)
```

The coefficients in @tbl-lm show the direction and size of these effects with the other characteristics held fixed. Each additional 100 days before the election was associated with about `r round(b_day12, 1)` more points of error in 2012 and `r round(b_day16, 1)` more in 2016. In 2012, Internet polls had about `r abs(round(b_int12, 1))` fewer points of error, while the other 2012 modes did not differ significantly. In 2016 the only significant mode difference was for the rare "Other" modes (`r round(b_oth16, 1)` more points of error). This group contains only 26 polls before the train/test split, and combines mail, mixed-mode and live phone/online polls, so it should be interpreted carefully. In 2016, a poll with 1,000 more respondents had about `r abs(round(coef(full16)["n1000"], 1))` fewer points of error, and polls in the "Pollster" partisanship category had about `r abs(round(coef(full16)["partisanshipPollster"], 1))` fewer points of error than non-partisan polls. Polls in the "Sponsor" category did not differ from non-partisan polls, and none of these effects were present in 2012. Overall the models explain little of the variation in error (95% confidence intervals for parameters can be found in @tbl-model-detail, code in @sec-app-linear).

@fig-diag12 and @fig-diag16 check the model assumptions. There are some concerns of heteroscedasticity, with variability increasing as fitted values increase and violations of normality, especially in upper tails. Cook's distance remained below approximately 0.1 in both elections, though some polls exceeded the 4/n guideline.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diag12
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the 2012 linear model of absolute margin error: residuals against fitted values, normal Q-Q plot, scale-location plot, and Cook's distance (dashed line at 4/n)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
# Four standard diagnostics for one fitted model
diag_plots <- function(m, yr) {
  par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
  plot(m, which = 1, sub.caption = yr)   # residuals vs fitted
  plot(m, which = 2, sub.caption = yr)   # normal Q-Q
  plot(m, which = 3, sub.caption = yr)   # scale-location
  plot(cooks.distance(m), type = "h", ylab = "Cook's distance",
       main = paste("Cook's distance,", yr))
  abline(h = 4 / nobs(m), col = "red", lty = 2)
  par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
}
diag_plots(full12, "2012")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-diag16
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the 2016 linear model of absolute margin error: residuals against fitted values, normal Q-Q plot, scale-location plot, and Cook's distance (dashed line at 4/n)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
diag_plots(full16, "2016")
```

Multicollinearity was found to not be a concern. Analysis of this can be found in @sec-app-linear.

## Predicting the size of the error on new polls

On the testing set, the models explained little of the error. Out-of-sample R² was `r r2_lm("2012", "Test")`% in 2012 and `r r2_lm("2016", "Test")`% in 2016, against `r r2_lm("2012", "Train")`% and `r r2_lm("2016", "Train")`% in training. The negative 2016 value means the model predicted the test polls no better than the average training error (@tbl-test-lm).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-test-lm
#| tbl-cap: "Prediction of absolute margin error (percentage points) on the training and test polls. R² is measured against predicting the training mean, so values near zero (or negative) mean the model predicts no better than the average error. MAE represents the error in predicting the absolute error."
lm_eval %>%
  select(Year, Model, Set, MAE, R2) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Set, values_from = c(MAE, R2), names_glue = 
                "{.value} ({Set})") %>% 
  rename_with(~ gsub("R2", "R²", .x)) %>% 
  kable(digits = 3)
```

## Unexpected results and influential polls

@tbl-influence-counts shows that very few polls are considered outliers (greater than 3 standard deviations from the model's prediction), though some are above the 4/n Cook's distance diagnostic. The most influential polls, seen in @tbl-influence-top, mostly have both large actual margins and errors. Outliers, which make up about 1-2% of polls, are slightly more common among incorrect polls (@tbl-outlier-winner), and the polls with the greatest studentised residuals are found in 2016 (@fig-outlier-winner). @tbl-sensitivity shows that refitting without influential training polls did not improve test performance, whereas excluding the unexpected test polls lowered the 2012 test RMSE from 2.84 to 2.65, so a few outlying polls account for a noticeable share of the error. Code can be found in @sec-Inf-Sens.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-influence-counts
#| tbl-cap: "Number of unusual and potentially influential training polls."
#| echo: false

bind_rows(
  `2012` = inf12,
  `2016` = inf16,
  .id = "Election"
) %>%
  group_by(Election) %>%
  summarise(
    Polls = n(),
    Outliers = sum(outlier),
    Influential = sum(influential),
    `Largest Cook's D` = max(cooks),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-influence-top
#| tbl-cap: "Five most influential training polls in each election, ranked by Cook's distance."
#| echo: false
bind_rows(
  `2012` = inf12,
  `2016` = inf16,
  .id = "Election"
) %>%
  group_by(Election) %>%
  slice_max(cooks, n = 5) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    state = state.abb[match(
      str_to_title(state),
      state.name
    )]
  ) %>%
  select(
    Election, state, mode3, sample_size,
    days_to_election, dem, rep, act_margin,
    abs_err, stud, cooks
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
  digits = 2,
  align = c("c", "c", "l", rep("r", 8)),
  col.names = c(
    "Election\\hspace{0.5em}", "State", "Mode", "Sample size",
    "Days to election", "Poll Dem %",
    "Poll Rep %", "Actual margin",
    "Absolute error", "Studentised residual",
    "Cook's D"
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-outlier-winner
#| tbl-cap: "Frequency of statistical outliers among polls that correctly and incorrectly predicted the winner."
#| echo: false

bind_rows(
  `2012` = inf12,
  `2016` = inf16,
  .id = "Election"
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(correct)) %>%
  group_by(Election) %>%
  summarise(
    `Correct polls` = sum(correct == 1),
    `Incorrect polls` = sum(correct == 0),
    `Outliers among correct (%)` =
      100 * mean(outlier[correct == 1]),
    `Outliers among incorrect (%)` =
      100 * mean(outlier[correct == 0]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-outlier-winner
#| fig-cap: "Studentised residuals against fitted absolute error, separated by whether the poll correctly predicted the winner. Dashed lines indicate the ±3 outlier thresholds."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| echo: false

bind_rows(
  `2012` = inf12,
  `2016` = inf16,
  .id = "Election"
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(correct)) %>%
  mutate(
    Outcome = if_else(
      correct == 1,
      "Right winner",
      "Wrong winner"
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(fitted, stud, colour = Outcome)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(-3, 3),
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Election) +
  labs(
    x = "Fitted absolute error (percentage points)",
    y = "Studentised residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of test-set prediction performance to influential training polls and unusually inaccurate test polls. Outliers were considered as polls greater than three residual standard errors from the model's prediction. There were no outliers in the 2016 testing set."

bind_rows(s12, s16) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  rename("R²" = R2) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Accuracy in picking the winning candidate

On the testing polls, the logistic models do not beat the benchmark of assuming every poll picks the right winner. In 2012 the model never predicted a wrong winner, so its accuracy (`r round(100 * logit_eval$Accuracy[1], 1)`%) equals the majority-class rate, defined as the more common outcome in the training polls (right or wrong winner). The model's AUC (`r round(logit_eval$AUC[1], 2)`) is close to 0.5, which indicates a model little better than chance. In 2016 the AUC was higher (`r round(get_le("2016", "Full", "AUC"), 2)`), but accuracy (`r round(100 * get_le("2016", "Full", "Accuracy"), 1)`%) was below the benchmark (`r round(100 * get_le("2016", "Full", "Majority-class accuracy"), 1)`%). Only `r n_flag16_wrong` of the `r n_flag16` polls the full model flagged as likely wrong (predicted probability of a right winner below 0.5) were wrong, so flagging polls as incorrect was actually worse than chance (@tbl-test-logit). Confusion tables can be found in @tbl-confusion, code in @sec-app-logistic, @sec-app-evaluation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-test-logit
#| tbl-cap: "Performance of the logistic models at predicting whether a poll picked the right winner, on the test polls. Accuracy uses a 0.5 cut-off and is compared with always predicting the majority class; AUC of 0.5 means no discrimination."
kable(logit_eval, digits = 3)
```

The two accuracy measures (binary and percentage) exhibit different behaviour (@fig-binary-pct, @tbl-race). Polls in states where the actual margin was 20+ points had the largest margin errors (6.1 and 8.7 points), yet almost always picked the winner (100% and 99.2%).

```{r}
#| label: fig-binary-pct
#| fig-cap: "Absolute margin error against the size of the actual margin. A poll can only pick the wrong winner if its error exceeds the actual margin, so wrong-winner polls lie above the dashed line."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
polls %>%
  filter(!is.na(correct)) %>%
  mutate(outcome = factor(correct, levels = c(1, 0), labels = 
                            c("Right winner", "Wrong winner"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(abs(act_margin), abs_err, colour = outcome)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(x = "Actual margin (absolute, percentage points)",
       y = "Absolute margin error (percentage points)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-race
#| tbl-cap: "Mean absolute margin error and percentage of polls picking the right winner, by how close the actual result was."
polls %>%
  filter(!is.na(correct)) %>%
  mutate(`Actual margin` = cut(abs(act_margin), breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 20, Inf), 
                          right = FALSE, labels =
                          c("< 5", "5 to 10", "10 to 20", "20 +"))) %>%
  group_by(Year = year, `Actual margin`) %>%
  summarise(Polls = n(),
            `Mean absolute error` = mean(abs_err),
            `Right winner (%)` = 100 * mean(correct),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  kable(digits = 1)
```

## Adjusting polling margins 
The predicted error by the models is subtracted from the original polling margin to generate adjusted predictions across both elections. We also apply a constant mean adjustment, subtracting the average signed error of the training data from every polling margin. Code can be found in @sec-app-signed, @sec-app-adjustments.

```{r}
#| label: bias-adjustment
#| include: false
# Keep only the polling modes that appear in both elections' models
common_modes <- intersect(step12s$xlevels$mode3,
                          step16s$xlevels$mode3)

common_modes <- setdiff(common_modes, "Other")

t12s <- test12 %>% filter(mode3 %in% common_modes)
t16s <- test16 %>% filter(mode3 %in% common_modes)

check_bias <- function(model, test) {
  original = test$dem - test$rep
  adjusted = original - predict(model, newdata = test)
  actual = test$act_margin
  
  data.frame(
    method = c("Original", "Adjusted"),
    MAE = c(mean(abs(original - actual)),
            mean(abs(adjusted - actual))),
    winner_accuracy = c(mean(sign(original) == sign(actual)),
                        mean(sign(adjusted) == sign(actual)))
  )
}
bias_results <- bind_rows(
  "2012 on 2012" = check_bias(step12s, t12s),
  "2016 on 2016" = check_bias(step16s, t16s),
  "2012 on 2016" = check_bias(step12s, t16s),
  "2016 on 2012" = check_bias(step16s, t12s),
  .id = "Comparison"
)

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bias
#| tbl-cap: "Mean absolute error (MAE, percentage points) and winner accuracy of the original poll margins and of margins adjusted by a stepwise model of signed error, on the test polls. 'A on B' means the model fitted to A's training polls was applied to B's test polls. MAE represents the polling error itself."

knitr::kable(bias_results, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Comparison", "Method", "MAE", "Winner Accuracy"))
```

```{r}
#| label: mean-adjustment
#| include: false
check_mean <- function(train, test) {

  original <- test$dem - test$rep
  adjusted <- original - mean(train$signed_err)

  c(
    MAE = mean(abs(adjusted - test$act_margin)),
    Winner_Accuracy = mean(sign(adjusted) ==
                           sign(test$act_margin))
  )
}


mean_results <- rbind(
  "2012 on 2012" = check_mean(d12s, t12s),
  "2016 on 2016" = check_mean(d16s, t16s),
  "2012 on 2016" = check_mean(d12s, t16s),
  "2016 on 2012" = check_mean(d16s, t12s)
)

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bias-mean
#| tbl-cap: "Mean absolute error (MAE, percentage points) and winner accuracy after subtracting the average signed error of the training polls from every test poll's margin. 'A on B' means the average error from A's training polls was applied to B's test polls."

mean_results %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Comparison") %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Comparison", "MAE", "Winner Accuracy"))

```

```{r}
#| label: bias-tests
#| include: false
# 2012 polling margins
original <- t12s$dem - t12s$rep
actual <- t12s$act_margin

# Errors after mean and regression correction
err_mean <- abs(original - mean(d12s$signed_err) - actual)
err_model <- abs(original - predict(step12s, newdata = t12s) - actual)

# Paired t-test
tt12 <- t.test(err_mean, err_model, paired = TRUE)

# 2016 polling margins
original <- t16s$dem - t16s$rep
actual <- t16s$act_margin

# Errors after mean and regression correction
err_mean <- abs(original - mean(d16s$signed_err) - actual)
err_model <- abs(original - predict(step16s, newdata = t16s) - actual)

# Paired t-test
tt16 <- t.test(err_mean, err_model, paired = TRUE)

# Actual and predicted signed errors
actual16 <- (t16s$dem - t16s$rep) - t16s$act_margin
pred16 <- predict(step16s, newdata = t16s)

r16 <- cor(actual16, pred16)

```

Both models improved the internal polling accuracy. For 2012 polling MAE fell from `r round(bias_results$MAE[1], 3)` to `r round(bias_results$MAE[2], 3)` with model adjustment and `r round(mean_results["2012 on 2012", "MAE"], 3)` with constant mean adjustment. In 2016, MAE fell from `r round(bias_results$MAE[3], 3)` to `r round(bias_results$MAE[4], 3)` and `r round(mean_results["2016 on 2016", "MAE"], 3)` respectively. The 2012 regression adjustment significantly outperformed the constant mean adjustment (paired t-test, p = `r round(tt12$p.value, 3)`), but in 2016 it did not (p = `r round(tt16$p.value, 3)`). Winner accuracy also improved under both methods, suggesting that correcting polling bias improves predictions when election results are already known. Predicted and actual signed errors in 2016 were almost uncorrelated (r = `r round(r16, 2)`).

cross-election adjustments were less effective. Applying one election's model to the other increased MAE in both directions (@tbl-bias), and the constant-mean correction did the same (@tbl-bias-mean).

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

We were unable to determine the accuracy of a poll based on its characteristics. Linear models explained just `r r2_lm("2012", "Test")`% of the variation in margin error in 2012 and `r r2_lm("2016", "Test")`% in 2016 (@tbl-test-lm) on testing polls. This indicates that the models offered little predictive value, performing no better than simply predicting the average error in 2016. Similarly, the logistic models did not outperform the baseline strategy of assuming that every poll would correctly predict the winner (@tbl-test-logit). We also found no significant relationship between the sampled population (likely or registered voters) and poll accuracy in either election (p = `r sprintf("%.2f", p_pop12)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", p_pop16)`).

Despite the models' limited predictive performance, some poll characteristics were associated with accuracy. Timing showed the clearest and most consistent relationship: for every additional 100 days between a poll and the election, margin error increased by approximately `r round(b_day12, 1)` points in 2012 and `r round(b_day16, 1)` points in 2016. This is unsurprising, as public opinion can shift throughout a campaign, making earlier polls less reliable. Polling mode was also significant in both elections, although the results differed. Internet polls were approximately `r abs(round(b_int12, 1))` points more accurate than live phone polls in 2012, but this advantage was not evident in 2016. In 2016, larger sample sizes were associated with lower errors, however this relationship was not significant in 2012. It is important to note that because the data collected was observational, these relationships indicate associations rather than evidence that changing a poll's characteristics would necessarily improve its accuracy.

The models' low explanatory power suggests that poll characteristics alone cannot account for much of the variation in polling error, likely reflecting random sampling variation. There is also evidence that polling errors were partly shared across polls within an election. For example, in 2016, subtracting the average bias from each poll reduced mean absolute error from `r round(bias_results$MAE[3], 1)` to `r round(mean_results["2016 on 2016", "MAE"], 1)` points. However, adjustments based on one election increased error when applied to the other. This suggests that polling errors may reflect election-specific circumstances, limiting the extent to which adjustments estimated from one election can be generalised to another.

The two accuracy measures behave differently. Polls in lopsided races had large margin errors but still picked the winner, whereas in close races only `r pct_close16`% of 2016 polls did (@tbl-race). Winner accuracy therefore depends mainly on how close the race was, so the characteristics that explain margin error need not help predict the winner.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, polls conducted in the same state are not independent, which may inflate p-values. Second, skewness of residuals may affect linear model assumptions. Third, our random train/test split meant that polls in the test set could come from the same states and pollsters represented in the training set, which could overstate predictability for unknown pollsters or states. Sensitivity analysis showed that removing influential training polls did not improve test performance. A few unexpectedly inaccurate polls inflated test error in 2012, so occasional outliers may limit how well a model can predict poll error.

Future research could investigate whether state-level and pollster-specific characteristics provide greater predictive value than the polling methods examined here. It could also examine how polling error changes throughout an election campaign and whether patterns observed across multiple elections can be used to improve the predictions of future polling accuracy.

## Linear regression analysis {#sec-app-linear}

Multiple linear regression models were fitted separately for 2012 and 2016. The following code includes model fitting, ANOVA, model selection, influence diagnostics and lastly response transformations.

Multicollinearity was not a concern: the largest $\text{GVIF}^{1/(2\,\text{Df})}$ was `r round(max(v12[, "GVIF^(1/(2*Df))"]), 2)` in 2012 and `r round(max(v16[, "GVIF^(1/(2*Df))"]), 2)` in 2016, well below the usual threshold of about 2.2 (equivalent to a VIF of 5). Box-Cox estimated a power of `r round(bc12[1, "Est Power"], 2)` in 2012 and `r round(bc16[1, "Est Power"], 2)` in 2016, between a log transformation (0) and a square root (0.5). The square root is the nearest standard transformation, so we used it in the refit in @tbl-test-lm.
